content: I'm a complete novice at music theory. Why do two nearby piano notes sound harsh together? I assume dissonance means someone has played the wrong notes, but composers seem to use those combinations deliberately, so what exactly makes the sound feel rough?

Dissonance does not mean the notes are wrong. Nearby notes can create closely spaced sound waves that alternately reinforce and cancel one another, producing audible beating or roughness. Your ear often interprets that activity as unstable. Composers use it deliberately because instability can create motion: a rough combination can make the smoother chord that follows feel settled and convincing.

What is that beating in ordinary terms? Is it an extra note created between the two keys, or is the volume actually wobbling? I can hear a kind of pulsing when notes are close, but the pitches themselves still seem separate.

It is mainly a wobble in loudness, not a new played note. Each pitch makes a repeating pressure pattern in the air. When two patterns are close in speed, they drift in and out of alignment. They add together when aligned and partly cancel when opposed, so the combined sound repeatedly grows and shrinks.

Then why can two notes farther apart still sound tense? A low C and the F-sharp above it are not crowded together on the keyboard. Does each piano note contain smaller hidden sounds that can still bump into one another?

Yes. A piano note contains a fundamental pitch plus quieter overtones above it. Even when two fundamentals are far apart, some of their overtones may land close together and create roughness. There is also a learned, musical side: listeners recognize some intervals as less settled because of how those intervals behave within familiar scales and chords.

So if a violin and a flute play the same pair of notes, should the chord feel equally dissonant? Their tones sound different to me, which makes me think the hidden sounds might change the amount of roughness.

It may not feel equally rough. Violin and flute tones emphasize different overtones, so the clashes among those overtones differ. Loudness, register, and tone quality matter too. Yet the interval still carries a recognizable harmonic role, so changing instruments can soften or sharpen the sensory roughness without completely changing whether the combination feels stable in context.

I'm new to music theory. Why does changing one note turn a cheerful major chord into a gloomy minor chord? Minor keys are just sad major keys, as far as I understand, but I do not see how such a small change causes that effect.

The small change alters the chord's pattern of distances. In C major, C to E spans four semitones; in C minor, C to E-flat spans three. That lower middle note changes how the chord's frequencies and overtones combine. Major and minor often carry bright and dark associations, but they are not fixed emotional labels: tempo, melody, rhythm, register, and culture can outweigh the chord quality.

What does the middle note actually do that the bottom and top notes do not? I had assumed a chord's mood came from whether all three notes were generally high or low, rather than from the spacing inside it.

The bottom note gives the chord its root, and the top note is commonly a fifth above it. Those two are identical in major and minor triads. The middle note, called the third, identifies the quality: a major third produces a major triad, while a minor third produces a minor triad. Overall pitch height changes color, but not that basic identity.

Does that mean a minor chord is more dissonant than a major chord because its middle note is closer to the bottom one? It sounds darker to me, so I have been treating darkness and dissonance as the same thing.

Not necessarily. Both major and minor triads are usually treated as consonant because each can sound stable and complete. Darkness describes a perceived color or association; dissonance describes roughness or harmonic instability. A minor triad can be dark yet settled, while a bright-sounding chord can contain a strongly dissonant note that demands resolution.

Why do songs in minor sometimes end on a major chord, then? If major and minor are chord types rather than simple moods, is that last brightening changing the key, or only changing the final chord for effect?

Often it is only a final alteration, traditionally called a Picardy third. A piece in a minor key ends by raising the third of its final tonic chord, making that chord major. The surrounding melody and earlier harmony still establish the minor key. The effect can sound like illumination or closure, but it does not retroactively turn the whole piece into major.
If the same minor chord can sound settled in one place and uneasy in another, what should I listen for to separate the chord's basic color from the job it is doing in the song?

First hear whether the chord itself is major or minor by focusing on its third. Then notice its position relative to the home chord. A minor tonic can feel fully at rest; the same shape built on another scale step may feel temporary. Also listen to the bass and the next chord, since expectation and movement reveal function more clearly than color alone.

I'm a beginner with harmony. What makes simple chords sound pleasant in the first place? I have heard that notes fit when their vibrations divide evenly, so is consonance basically the ear noticing clean fractions and dissonance noticing messy ones?

Clean frequency ratios are part of the explanation, but not the whole story. An octave has a 2:1 ratio and a perfect fifth roughly 3:2, so many of their overtones coincide. That can reduce roughness and make the blend easy to hear as one unit. Still, tuning systems, musical context, familiarity, tone color, and culture also shape judgments of consonance.

Why do matching overtones matter to the ear? Are they physically combining into one smoother wave, or does the brain decide that several sounds probably came from the same object and group them together?

Both ideas contribute. Coinciding overtones reinforce stable repeating patterns and avoid some of the rapid interference that creates roughness. The auditory system is also good at grouping frequencies that follow one harmonic pattern, because natural sound sources often produce exactly that structure. A consonant interval can therefore be physically smoother and easier for the brain to organize.

What happens with an ordinary piano, where the tuning is adjusted so every key works? The fractions cannot all stay exact. Shouldn't familiar consonant chords become slightly dissonant once those neat ratios are bent?

They do become slightly less pure. Modern pianos generally use equal temperament, which makes most intervals a little wider or narrower than simple ratios. The compromise lets musicians play in every key without retuning. Familiar fifths and thirds remain close enough to their pure versions to sound consonant, though careful listeners can hear slow beating, especially in sustained intervals.

Does everyone therefore agree on which chords are consonant, apart from small tuning differences? I am unsure whether the pleasantness is built into hearing or learned from hearing the same kinds of songs repeatedly.

There is broad agreement about extreme cases, especially when sensory roughness is obvious, but the boundary is flexible. Hearing provides shared constraints: beating and overtone interactions affect human ears similarly. Musical exposure teaches expectations about which combinations are stable, expressive, or ordinary. A chord can be acoustically rough yet become stylistically familiar enough that listeners no longer hear it as mistaken.

Then what is a good test for the difference between physical roughness and learned tension? If I hold a chord by itself, would that reveal the roughness, while placing it inside a tune reveals what I have learned to expect?

That is a useful comparison. Sustain the chord alone, preferably with a steady tone, and listen for buzzing, beating, or crowded frequencies; those point toward sensory roughness. Then place it before several possible following chords. If one continuation feels strongly expected, that pull reflects learned harmonic function. The two effects interact, so the test separates them only approximately.

Would playing the same chord very softly change that test? Harsh combinations often seem less bothersome when quiet, so I wonder whether loudness changes consonance itself or merely makes the clashing parts harder to notice.

Softening a chord often reduces perceived roughness because the ear responds differently across loudness levels, and quieter partials may fall below audibility. The interval relationships remain unchanged, so its harmonic function can persist even as the sensory clash weakens. This is one reason orchestration and dynamics can make the same written harmony feel gentle in one passage and abrasive in another.

I'm a total novice at chords. Why does a tense chord seem to want another chord after it? Notes cannot literally want anything, so I assume the final chord simply removes the wrong notes and replaces them with the correct ones.

The sense of wanting comes from expectation, not intention. Some notes sit close to notes in a more stable chord, and familiar musical patterns teach you to expect them to move there. The tense notes are not wrong; they are doing a job. When they shift by small steps into a stable arrangement, the contrast creates the feeling of release.
What makes the destination stable? Is it just the chord used most often in the song, or does it have a special arrangement of notes that would sound finished even if I heard it without the rest?

Usually both sound structure and context help. The home chord, or tonic, has relatively consonant internal intervals, so it can sound settled by itself. Repetition, melody, and bass movement also establish it as the center of a particular piece. Without context, several major or minor chords might sound equally complete; the preceding music tells you which one counts as home.

Why is the chord built on the fifth note especially good at leading home? I hear people describe that chord as dominant, but to me it just sounds like another stack of three notes until the home chord follows.

The dominant contains notes with efficient paths into the tonic. In C major, the G chord contains B, which lies one semitone below C and strongly tends upward. Its bass, G, also relates closely to C through the fifth. Adding F creates a dominant seventh: B and F form an unstable interval, and each can move by step into the tonic chord.
If I stop after that dominant seventh and never play the home chord, is the dissonance still there? Or is dissonance only the feeling caused by knowing what chord was supposed to come next?

Some dissonance remains in the isolated chord because its notes, especially the seventh and the interval called a tritone, can sound rough or unsettled. Context adds directional tension by suggesting a likely continuation. So one part is present in the sound itself, while another part comes from an expectation that the music deliberately leaves unanswered.

Can a composer make that same dominant seventh sound like a resting place by repeating it long enough? I am trying to tell whether repetition can turn any wrong-sounding group into something consonant, or only make it familiar.

Repetition can make the chord feel familiar and can weaken your expectation of an immediate resolution, but it does not erase every acoustic feature. The close interactions among its notes remain. A composer can also change the bass, spacing, instrumentation, or surrounding harmony so the chord functions as a stable color rather than a command to move home.
What does changing the spacing mean here? If the notes keep the same letter names, why would moving one of them an octave higher make the chord less harsh or change how strongly it seems to pull?

Spacing changes which frequencies and overtones crowd one another. Low notes placed close together often sound muddy because their lower overtones interact within a sensitive range; spreading them across octaves can clarify the chord. The note names and harmonic function remain, but the sensory roughness changes. Moving a tendency note into a prominent upper voice can also make its expected resolution easier to hear.

So when I hear a chord as unpleasant, what should I check first: the distance between its notes, how loudly it is played, or whether the surrounding chords make it feel unfinished? Those seem like different causes with the same result.

Check them separately. First isolate the chord and vary its register, spacing, instrument, and loudness; changes there reveal sensory roughness. Next keep its sound fixed but place it in different progressions; changes in its pull reveal harmonic expectation. Finally notice personal or stylistic familiarity. What feels unpleasant usually combines these layers rather than coming from a single rule.
